definition: Disheartened means having lost hope, courage, morale, or enthusiasm.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word disheartened. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know disheartened should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Missing the qualifying time by nine seconds left Amara so disheartened that she almost skipped her next training run.
A disappointed person feels let down for a moment, while a disheartened person has lost real hope and enthusiasm for continuing.
Disheartened spirits droop but can recover, while a despairing person has given up hope entirely.

Discouraged means your confidence about succeeding has slipped - the task now looks bigger than your ability. Disheartened is a broader deflation: hope, courage, and enthusiasm all drain away together after a setback. A discouraged student doubts she can pass; a disheartened one has trouble caring enough to open the book.

Dejected describes visible sadness - slumped shoulders and a downcast face right after a blow. It is about low spirits in the moment. Disheartened reaches forward: the setback has drained your hope and enthusiasm for continuing. You look dejected at the result; you feel disheartened about trying again.

Demoralized means morale has collapsed, and it usually describes a group ground down under sustained pressure - a losing team, an exhausted staff. Disheartened is the gentler, more personal word for one person's hope and enthusiasm draining away after a setback. An army is demoralized; a lone baker counting slow mornings is disheartened.

Three months after opening, Tomas counted another slow morning at his bakery and felt thoroughly disheartened.
He had imagined lines out the door, not trays of unsold bread, and it took real effort to preheat the ovens the next day.
Tomas has lost hope and enthusiasm after his expectations collapsed, which is exactly the deflated feeling that disheartened describes.
Disheartened is about morale: hope, courage, and enthusiasm draining away after a setback.

Unlike disaffected, which means a person or group has lost loyalty to an authority and turned rebellious, disheartened carries no rebellion at all; a disheartened person may still be completely loyal, just deflated.

Devon spent the fall building a water filter for the regional science fair, testing it nightly at the kitchen sink.
At the judging, a wiring fault he had never seen before shut the pump down twenty seconds into his demonstration.
He was not angry, his mother noticed.
It was quieter than that: for weeks afterward he was simply disheartened.
The filter sat untouched in the garage.
He stopped reading the electronics forum he had checked every morning, and when his teacher mentioned next year's fair, he changed the subject.
It was not that he doubted he could fix the pump.
The wanting-to had drained out of him.
